# Support Resolution Engine — Prospecting Batch 2026-10-05

## Objective
Convert the existing Support Resolution Engine into the first paid pilot. No new product work is authorized before buyer signal.

## High-priority prospects

### 1. DZ Ecommerce — Algeria
- Public signal: their site explicitly describes merchants being overwhelmed by unread DMs, manual order confirmation, and spreadsheet-based order handling.
- Contact: contact@dz-ecommerce.com
- Phone: +213 775 30 80 80
- Fit: HIGH — local COD + WhatsApp + order context are directly aligned with the resolver workflow.
- Evidence: https://dz-ecommerce.com/en and https://dz-ecommerce.com/en/delivery-partners
- Proposed pilot: 7–14 days, human-approved support resolution for a narrow ticket class.
- Initial commercial anchor: $1,000 pilot, 50% upfront.

### 2. DZBuild — Algeria
- Public signal: Algerian ecommerce platform with active merchant stores, team access, order management, API v1 and webhook capability.
- Contact: support@dzbuild.com
- Phone: +213 782 729 944
- Fit: HIGH — API/webhook boundary can support a controlled support workflow without inventing a new channel.
- Evidence: https://www.dzbuild.com/docs/intro and https://www.dzbuild.com/docs/operations/faq
- Proposed pilot: ticket triage + evidence-backed draft replies, initially human-reviewed.
- Initial commercial anchor: $1,000 pilot, 50% upfront.

### 3. Ordrate — MENA
- Public signal: orders arrive through WhatsApp and merchants follow up with customers there; platform has an active support/contact path.
- Contact: hello@ordrate.com
- Phone: +962 7 9671 7649
- Fit: MEDIUM-HIGH — WhatsApp/order-support workflow is directly relevant.
- Evidence: https://www.ordrate.com/
- Proposed pilot: order-status/support triage with human approval.
- Initial commercial anchor: $1,000 pilot, 50% upfront.

## Why these prospects
They have publicly visible support/order workflows rather than being generic AI leads. DZ Ecommerce is the strongest first target because its own public material describes the exact operational friction the Support Resolution Engine addresses.

## Sales boundary
- Do not claim existing customer savings.
- Do not claim live production integration.
- Do not promise autonomous outbound actions.
- Pilot starts with 3–10 redacted real cases.
- All responses remain drafts for customer review until explicit production approval.
- First paid gate: accepted scope + 50% upfront payment.

## Next state to record
Found opportunity → targeted outreach → client reply → call → proposal → invoice/payment → pilot.


### 4. Atlas Technology — Algeria (Oran)
- Public signal: Atlas CRM explicitly connects WhatsApp conversations, order confirmation, dispatch, delivery tracking, exceptions and COD reconciliation; Atlas also publishes a controlled pilot approach for real workflows.
- Contact: contact@atlas-technology-dz.com
- Phone: +213 541 89 83 81
- Fit: HIGH as a potential pilot/technology partner — the existing Atlas CRM workflow can provide the real operational context while EASY supplies an evidence-gated resolution layer.
- Evidence: https://atlas-technology-dz.com/solutions/atlas-crm and https://atlas-technology-dz.com/contact
- Proposed pilot: one narrow support/exception workflow, 7–14 days, human-reviewed drafts.
- Initial commercial anchor: $1,000 pilot, 50% upfront.
- Positioning: integration/augmentation of an existing operational system, not replacement.

### 5. Facile — Algeria
- Public signal: Facile explicitly targets Algerian merchants handling spreadsheets, WhatsApp orders and delivery apps, and advertises an Instagram/Messenger AI agent plus order/shipping workflows.
- Contact path: official site sales/enterprise contact.
- Fit: HIGH operational fit, but lower priority until a direct sales contact is identified.
- Evidence: https://facile-dz.com/
- Action: keep as a qualified prospect; do not send until a verified direct contact is available.

# Support Resolution Engine — Sales Kit

## 1. Offer
A human-supervised support automation service for repetitive customer-support tickets.

Workflow:
1. Ticket arrives.
2. Intent/category is identified.
3. Customer/order context is retrieved.
4. Relevant policy/context is applied.
5. Draft answer is generated.
6. Confidence/risk is assessed.
7. Safe cases can be resolved; uncertain or risky cases are escalated to a human.

We sell the business outcome: faster responses, fewer repetitive handling minutes, and measurable support efficiency. We do not sell an API.

## 2. First paid pilot
Recommended starting offer:
- Duration: 2–4 weeks
- Pilot price: USD 1,000
- One support workflow
- Human approval remains required for uncertain/risky cases
- Baseline captured before customization
- Controlled test set used before production rollout

Alternative commercial range: USD 500–2,000 depending on scope and integration work.

## 3. What the client receives
- Workflow assessment
- Support-ticket classification
- Policy-grounded response drafting
- Customer/order context retrieval using agreed data sources
- Confidence and escalation logic
- Pilot dashboard/report
- End-of-pilot KPI report
- Production recommendation

## 4. What is not included in the base pilot
- Full CRM/helpdesk replacement
- Unlimited custom integrations
- Autonomous handling of high-risk refunds, legal, medical, financial, or security cases
- Guaranteed savings or guaranteed automation percentage
- Customer-data processing before the appropriate access/security terms are agreed

## 5. Success metrics
Measure baseline and pilot performance for:
- First-response time
- Human minutes per ticket
- Safe-resolution rate
- Escalation rate
- Cost per resolved ticket
- Classification accuracy
- Draft acceptance/edit rate
- API/infrastructure cost per ticket

No ROI claim is made until baseline data is available.

## 6. Buyer
Primary: Head of Support / Customer Operations / COO.
Secondary: Support Director, CX Director, Operations Manager.

Best prospects have high ticket volume, repetitive questions, an existing helpdesk/CRM, and a clear support-cost problem.

## 7. Discovery questions
Ask only what is needed:
1. How many support tickets do you handle per month?
2. What are the top 5 repetitive ticket categories?
3. What helpdesk/CRM/order system do you use?
4. What percentage currently requires a human response?
5. What is the biggest support bottleneck: response time, staffing cost, backlog, or consistency?

## 8. Sales sequence
### Step 1 — Problem-first outreach
Do not lead with AI, APIs, or technical architecture.

Message structure:
- identify repetitive support workload
- state the measurable problem
- offer a short demonstration
- propose a pilot only after confirming fit

### Step 2 — 15-minute discovery
Confirm volume, repetitive categories, systems, current workflow, and baseline metrics.

### Step 3 — 3-minute demo
Show one ticket going from intake to classified intent, retrieved context, grounded draft, confidence, and escalation.

### Step 4 — Paid pilot
Send the proposal and invoice. Recommended payment: 50% at kickoff and 50% at pilot completion, unless the client requires another structure.

### Step 5 — Pilot
Use synthetic/sample data first where possible. Connect real customer data only after access/security requirements are agreed.

### Step 6 — ROI review
Compare baseline with pilot metrics. If the results are credible, propose production pricing.

## 9. Production pricing hypothesis
Starting point:
- Base: USD 750–2,500/month
- Plus usage where appropriate, such as per ticket/resolution
- Integration/setup fee when material integration work is required

Final price is based on volume, workflow complexity, integration scope, and measured value.

## 10. Payment setup
Preferred initial channel for an international client: PayPal Business, subject to account eligibility, client location, fees, and withdrawal availability. PayPal's Algeria business pages state that Business accounts can receive payments and provide invoicing/payment tools; PayPal's developer documentation lists Algeria as supported for business accounts. Verify the account's actual receiving/withdrawal capabilities before accepting a client payment.

Do not put payment credentials, API keys, or banking secrets in GitHub.

## 11. Proposal template

SERVICE PROPOSAL
Support Resolution Engine — Paid Pilot

Prepared for: [CLIENT NAME]
Prepared by: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
Date: [DATE]
Proposal valid until: [DATE]

Objective
Reduce repetitive support handling time while preserving human control over uncertain or high-risk cases.

Scope
- Ticket classification
- Customer/order context retrieval from agreed systems
- Policy-grounded response drafting
- Confidence/risk assessment
- Human escalation
- Pilot reporting

Duration
2–4 weeks.

Pilot investment
USD 1,000.

Payment terms
50% at kickoff; 50% at completion, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Success measures
The parties will agree baseline metrics before implementation. The pilot will report first-response time, human minutes/ticket, safe-resolution rate, escalation rate, accuracy, and operating cost.

Assumptions
Client provides the agreed sample data, policy documents, and access to required systems. Production access is subject to security/privacy approval.

Exclusions
No guarantee of a specific automation percentage or financial savings. High-risk actions remain human-controlled unless separately approved.

Acceptance
Client: ____________________
Name/Title: ________________
Date: ______________________

## 12. Invoice template

INVOICE
Invoice No.: SR-2026-001
Date: [DATE]
Due Date: [DATE]

From:
[YOUR BUSINESS / LEGAL NAME]
[ADDRESS]
[EMAIL]
[PHONE]
[BUSINESS REGISTRATION / TAX IDENTIFIERS IF APPLICABLE]

Bill To:
[CLIENT LEGAL NAME]
[CLIENT ADDRESS]
[CLIENT EMAIL]

Description:
Support Resolution Engine — 2–4 week paid pilot

Subtotal: USD 1,000
Taxes/VAT: [APPLICABLE TAX — CONFIRM WITH ACCOUNTANT]
Total Due: [TOTAL]

Payment method:
PayPal Business / [OTHER AGREED METHOD]
Payment reference: SR-2026-001

Terms:
50% due at kickoff; 50% due at completion, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Notes:
This invoice covers the defined pilot scope only. Production deployment, additional integrations, and ongoing usage are quoted separately.

## 13. Short outreach message

Subject: Reducing repetitive support workload

Hi [NAME],

I’m building a small support-operations solution for teams that handle a high volume of repetitive customer tickets.

It classifies incoming requests, retrieves the relevant customer/order context, prepares a policy-grounded response, and escalates uncertain cases to a human.

I’m offering a limited pilot where we measure the baseline first and then compare response time and human handling time against the pilot results.

If reducing repetitive support work is currently a priority for your team, I can show you the workflow in a few minutes.

Best,
[NAME]

## 14. Important legal/commercial note
This kit is a commercial starting point, not legal or tax advice. Before issuing a real invoice from Algeria, confirm the required legal entity, registration/tax identifiers, VAT treatment, invoicing requirements, foreign-currency/payment rules, and accounting treatment with an Algerian accountant or the relevant authority. The Algerian tax authority states that taxable businesses must issue an invoice or equivalent document and that invoices have specific identification and tax fields.

name: Bagisto commerce core smoke

on:
  push:
    paths:
      - "platform/commerce-core/**"
      - ".github/workflows/bagisto-commerce-core.yml"
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "platform/commerce-core/**"
      - ".github/workflows/bagisto-commerce-core.yml"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  bagisto-boot:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      database:
        image: mysql:8.0
        env:
          MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
          MYSQL_DATABASE: bagisto
        ports:
          - 3306:3306
        options: >-
          --health-cmd="mysqladmin ping -h 127.0.0.1 -proot"
          --health-interval=10s
          --health-timeout=5s
          --health-retries=10

    steps:
      - name: Checkout EASY integration contract
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Checkout pinned Bagisto
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: bagisto/bagisto
          ref: b40f998fa482dcbc99d24dccd4f45a263032100b
          path: .integration/bagisto

      - name: Verify pinned source
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: |
          test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "b40f998fa482dcbc99d24dccd4f45a263032100b"

      - name: Setup PHP
        uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: "8.3"
          extensions: curl, fileinfo, gd, intl, mbstring, openssl, pdo, pdo_mysql, tokenizer, zip
          tools: composer:v2

      - name: Install Bagisto
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist

      - name: Configure Bagisto
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: |
          cp .env.example .env
          sed -i "s|^APP_ENV=.*|APP_ENV=testing|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_CONNECTION=.*|DB_CONNECTION=mysql|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_HOST=.*|DB_HOST=127.0.0.1|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_PORT=.*|DB_PORT=3306|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_DATABASE=.*|DB_DATABASE=bagisto|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_USERNAME=.*|DB_USERNAME=root|" .env
          sed -i "s|^DB_PASSWORD=.*|DB_PASSWORD=root|" .env
          sed -i "s|^APP_URL=.*|APP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000|" .env

      - name: Install database and seed core
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: php artisan bagisto:install --no-interaction

      - name: Verify core routes
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: |
          php artisan route:list --json > /tmp/bagisto-routes.json
          php -r '
            $routes = json_decode(file_get_contents("/tmp/bagisto-routes.json"), true);
            $uris = array_column($routes, "uri");
            foreach (["/", "admin/login", "customer/register", "checkout/cart"] as $required) {
              if (!in_array($required, $uris, true)) {
                fwrite(STDERR, "Missing required route: {$required}\n");
                exit(1);
              }
            }
          '

      - name: Start Bagisto
        working-directory: .integration/bagisto
        run: |
          nohup php artisan serve --host=127.0.0.1 --port=8000 >/tmp/bagisto.log 2>&1 &
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do
            curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/ >/dev/null && exit 0
            sleep 2
          done
          cat /tmp/bagisto.log
          exit 1

      - name: Verify storefront and admin
        run: |
          curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/ >/dev/null
          curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/login >/dev/null
          curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:8000/customer/register >/dev/null

# Security Policy

## Security boundary
This repository must never contain live API keys, access tokens, OAuth client secrets, passwords, cookies, private certificates, customer credentials, or other private operational secrets.

Secrets belong in Replit/Railway/production secret management or protected environment variables, never in source files, issues, pull requests, logs, or documentation.

## Reporting a suspected leak
Do not copy or repost a suspected credential. Report the file/path and commit reference privately to `easy@agentmail.to` so it can be contained and rotated.

## Public disclosure boundary
Public content must remain limited to code and documentation that is safe to disclose. Runtime secrets, private customer data, internal credentials, and private operational material must remain outside the public repository.

## Remediation rule
Any real credential committed to Git history is treated as compromised and must be revoked/rotated before cleanup.

# SNIPER security integration

EASY adopts SNIPER as a defensive first-deviation security pattern for the product and its runtime boundaries.

SNIPER should observe authenticated, auditable signals such as:
- seller/admin identity and session changes
- new devices or network origins
- credential/token and permission changes
- API/webhook destination changes
- deployment/configuration/schema changes
- provider integration changes
- unexpected automation or agent/tool activity

A single anomaly is not treated as proof of compromise. Signals are correlated with approved changes, deployment provenance, and expected automation.

Response remains defensive: alert, step-up verification, revoke/rotate affected credentials, isolate an affected workload, preserve evidence, restore a known-good state, and independently verify recovery.

EASY must never use SNIPER for counter-intrusion, retaliation, or modification/deletion of third-party systems or data.

This document is an architectural integration note; runtime adapters should be added only where they can operate with least privilege and without introducing secrets into source control.

# EASY API Registry

The central API Bank for EASY. This repository stores discovery metadata and integration candidates; it does not store secrets.

## What is stored here

- Curated APIs and model providers relevant to EASY.
- Official documentation links.
- EASY priority (`P0` = immediate architecture relevance, `P1` = important, `P2` = later, `P3` = optional).
- Discovery sources for expanding the bank.
- Rules for evaluating providers before integration.

## EASY priority areas

1. AI / LLM
2. Vision / Product DNA / OCR
3. Image generation and editing
4. Video generation
5. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech
6. Web search and market research
7. E-commerce / product / pricing / reviews
8. Advertising and social platforms
9. Payments
10. Delivery and tracking
11. Maps / geocoding
12. Translation
13. Analytics
14. Moderation / safety
15. Product and barcode lookup

## Architecture rule

An API appearing in this registry does **not** mean EASY should integrate it immediately.

Production integrations must use provider-neutral adapters. Seller Flow must remain provider-agnostic, and Product Integrity must never be bypassed.

## Provider evaluation checklist

Before production integration, verify:

- API is currently available.
- Authentication mechanism and required scopes.
- Rate limits and quotas.
- Current pricing and free/trial limits.
- Commercial-use rights and model licenses.
- Privacy and data-retention behavior.
- Reliability and operational maturity.
- Input/output quality for the exact EASY task.
- Geographic availability, especially Algeria where relevant.
- Whether the provider supports the required image/video/text/audio formats.

## Secrets policy

**Never commit** API keys, access tokens, OAuth client secrets, passwords, cookies, private certificates or other credentials to GitHub.

Secrets belong in Replit Secrets/environment variables or another dedicated secret manager.

## Discovery sources

See `SOURCES.md` for the maintained list of public catalogs, official provider documentation and model discovery sources.

The bank is deliberately curated rather than blindly importing tens of thousands of APIs. A huge catalog is useful for discovery, but every production candidate must still be verified individually.

# API Lab

This is the experimental layer of the repository. Its purpose is to turn the API/knowledge bank into working prototypes rather than a static list.

## Rules
- Prefer no-key/free APIs for first experiments.
- Never commit secrets, API keys, OAuth tokens, cookies or credentials.
- Every experiment records: API, endpoint, capability, result, limitations, and a possible real-world use case.
- Experiments are disposable prototypes; production code must use provider-neutral adapters and explicit validation.

## First verified experiments

### 01 — Pokémon Explorer
- API: PokéAPI
- Endpoint tested: `/api/v2/pokemon/pikachu`
- Result: endpoint responded successfully during verification.
- Prototype: `mini-apps/pokemon-explorer.html`
- Useful for: testing API consumption, search UX, caching, image rendering and mobile UI.

### 02 — Card Battle
- API: Deck of Cards API
- Endpoint tested: `/api/deck/new/shuffle/?deck_count=1`
- Result: endpoint responded successfully during verification.
- Prototype: `mini-apps/card-battle.html`
- Useful for: game state, randomization, turn logic and API-backed game mechanics.

### 03 — Trivia Sprint
- API: Open Trivia Database
- Endpoint tested: `/api.php?amount=5&type=multiple`
- Result: endpoint responded successfully during verification.
- Prototype: `mini-apps/trivia-sprint.html`
- Useful for: quiz products, education, engagement loops and gamification.

## Company-problem experiments

The next experiments should target real operational pain, not just demos:

1. Customer-support triage — classify and route incoming questions.
2. Product catalog enrichment — turn incomplete product data into structured listings.
3. Market research — collect and normalize competitor/product signals.
4. Delivery visibility — normalize carrier tracking into one status model.
5. Ad creative intelligence — compare public ad signals and extract patterns.
6. Appointment/no-show reduction — reminders, status tracking and analytics.
7. Inventory alerts — detect low-stock/high-demand conditions.
8. Invoice/document extraction — convert documents into structured records.
9. Multilingual commerce — Arabic/French/English product and support workflows.
10. Internal knowledge assistant — answer staff questions from approved company documents.

Each problem will be converted into a small proof-of-concept before we consider production integration.

# Client Hunting & Offers Status — 2026-09-16

## Purpose
Persistent record for the `mony` Revenue Engine so client opportunities are not lost or confused with incoming client offers.

## Critical distinction
The opportunities found so far were **public paid job listings / prospecting opportunities**, not confirmed offers sent directly to the user by clients. No paid client deal, accepted proposal, or payment has been verified.

## Timeline
- **2026-09-11:** Paid opportunity matrix created. It identified 10 B2B service opportunities and defined the paid-pilot model. First experiments: Support Resolution Engine, Invoice/PO Exception Engine, RFQ-to-Quote Engine.
- **2026-09-12:** Additional paid opportunities were identified, including n8n/Voice AI agency work, a Spanish Upwork agency opportunity, lead generation, procurement automation, and B2B lead-gen. Services were mapped to concrete price ranges. Support Resolution Engine was framed as a $500–$2,000 pilot, with a $1,000 example, 50% upfront, 2–4 weeks.
- **2026-09-13 to 2026-09-15:** Client hunting/outreach work continued. Some direct outreach was sent, but there was no verified client reply or paid conversion. Some emails bounced (NuWorld/Teroin Labs/Agency Merlin). No verified follow-up reply was sent to those bounced addresses.
- **2026-09-16:** Review confirmed there was no evidence of an accepted paid offer or payment. Several strong public opportunities had not been submitted to yet.

## Opportunities specifically identified as still requiring submission at the latest review
1. WhatsApp AI Agent — listed around **$1,000**.
2. Spanish agency opportunity — around **$350 starting work**, with possible continuation.
3. Additional n8n/technical automation projects.

These are opportunities, not client offers, until a client responds/accepts.

## Outreach already recorded
Direct outreach was reported to:
- Virgin AI
- Korvox
- FloLogix
- tom@ana1.ae

Reported bounced addresses:
- NuWorld
- Teroin Labs
- Agency Merlin

At the latest verified review there was **no confirmed reply from these contacts** and no paid conversion.

## Was every offer answered?
**No — and the accurate reason is that there were not confirmed incoming client offers to answer.** The work consisted of discovering public opportunities and some outbound prospecting. The strongest discovered listings were not all submitted to, so it is incorrect to say that every opportunity was answered/applied to.

## Current sellability
There is a real service-selling path, but it is not yet a confirmed sale.

### Services that can currently be offered
- n8n/API integrations
- AI agents
- CRM/WhatsApp automation
- Document/data automation
- Testing and production hardening
- Voice/RAG/MCP integrations

### Primary productized offer
**Support Resolution Engine**
- Buyer: Head of Support / COO
- Pilot: 7–14 days for the narrow workflow; broader pilot model 2–4 weeks
- Example pilot pricing: **$1,000**, with earlier acceptable range **$500–$2,000**
- Payment model discussed: **50% upfront**
- Deliverable: ticket classification, context retrieval, policy-grounded draft response, confidence, escalation decision, measurable KPI
- Production hypothesis: roughly **$500–$2,500/month + usage**, depending on volume/integration

The repository's paid opportunity matrix also records Invoice/PO Exception Engine and RFQ-to-Quote Engine as concrete productized services.

## Commercial status
- Working demos/prototypes exist for parts of the service lab.
- The opportunity matrix defines buyer, workflow, KPI, pilot scope and pricing hypotheses.
- **No verified customer, signed proposal, paid pilot, or revenue yet.**
- Therefore: **sellable service concept + implementation capability = yes; confirmed market validation/revenue = no.**

## Rule for future client hunting
Never label a public listing as an incoming offer. Track separately:
1. Found opportunity
2. Application/proposal submitted
3. Client replied
4. Interview/call
5. Proposal accepted
6. Invoice/payment
7. Delivery
8. Recurring client

The goal of `mony` is to move opportunities through these states quickly and preserve evidence for each state.

# Paid Problem Lab

Goal: prioritize problems that companies already have budgets, owners, and measurable ROI for.

## Targeting rule

Do not build generic demos first. Prefer a problem when:

1. A company already spends money or staff time on it.
2. The buyer/owner is identifiable.
3. The problem repeats frequently.
4. The result can be measured in revenue, cost, time, errors, risk, or retention.
5. Existing APIs can reduce implementation cost and time.
6. We can produce a small proof of value before asking for a larger contract.

## Highest-priority paid problem families

### P0 — B2B commerce operations
- Quote/RFQ generation and response automation.
- Product/catalog data cleanup and enrichment.
- Inventory availability synchronization.
- Contract/pricing-rule extraction and validation.
- Order routing and fulfillment exception handling.
- Customer support resolution and ticket triage.
- Product search and recommendation quality.

Why: current 2026 B2B research identifies data quality, product/inventory/customer data, quoting, pricing and operational automation as high-value problems with active investment.

### P0 — Customer support
- Classify incoming tickets automatically.
- Retrieve the correct company policy/order information.
- Draft replies with human approval.
- Detect refunds, cancellations and escalation cases.
- Measure resolution time and cost per resolution.

Commercial model: setup fee + monthly platform/usage fee, or savings/recovered-revenue share where appropriate.

### P0 — Logistics
- Shipment exception detection.
- Proactive customer notifications.
- Failed-delivery analysis.
- Carrier comparison and routing support.
- Quote-to-cash workflow automation.
- Document/invoice extraction.

Commercial model: per shipment, per location, or monthly enterprise subscription.

### P1 — Revenue and sales operations
- Lead qualification.
- Proposal/RFQ preparation.
- CRM data cleanup.
- Meeting-to-CRM extraction.
- Sales intelligence and account research.
- Pricing and quote consistency checks.

### P1 — Finance/back office
- Invoice extraction and reconciliation.
- Purchase-order matching.
- Expense/document classification.
- Payment exception detection.
- Recurring reporting automation.

### P1 — Marketing and advertising
- Creative/ad-library intelligence.
- Campaign anomaly detection.
- Competitor creative monitoring.
- Product-feed quality checks.
- Landing-page/content QA.
- Automated performance reporting.

### P1 — SaaS monetization
- Usage metering.
- Pricing/package configuration.
- Entitlement checks.
- AI usage billing.
- Revenue leakage detection.

## Buyer map

| Problem | Likely buyer | KPI proving value |
|---|---|---|
| Support automation | COO / Head of Support | cost per resolution, response time, resolution rate |
| Quote automation | CRO / Sales Ops | quote turnaround, win rate, rep hours |
| Inventory/data quality | COO / Ecommerce | error rate, conversion, stock accuracy |
| Logistics exceptions | COO / Logistics | failed deliveries, support tickets, cost/shipment |
| Invoice reconciliation | CFO / Finance Ops | processing time, exception rate, labor cost |
| Pricing/monetization | CFO / CPO / CTO | time-to-price-change, revenue leakage, engineering hours |
| Ad intelligence | CMO / Growth | ROAS, creative testing speed, analyst hours |

## Experiment protocol

For every target problem, create a tiny working prototype using the API bank:

1. Define the company problem in one sentence.
2. Identify the current manual workflow.
3. Identify the buyer and existing budget owner.
4. Select 1–3 APIs only.
5. Build a narrow prototype.
6. Test with synthetic or public data first.
7. Measure one business KPI.
8. Record API cost, latency, failure modes, privacy/licensing constraints.
9. Estimate customer ROI.
10. Keep only experiments with a credible paid path.

## Scoring

Score each opportunity from 1–5 for:

- Pain severity
- Existing spend
- Frequency
- Buyer clarity
- Measurable ROI
- API feasibility
- Prototype speed
- Integration difficulty (reverse score)
- Competition (reverse score)
- Compliance risk (reverse score)

Prioritize opportunities with the highest combined score and a clear buyer.

## Important distinction

A technically impressive API demo is not automatically a business opportunity. The lab exists to discover **paid problems**, not merely interesting technology.

## Current research signal

2026 B2B commerce research reports active AI spending, with data quality remaining a major barrier and operational workflows such as quoting, inventory and pricing showing measurable improvement from automation. Logistics research likewise points to cost reduction and customer-service automation as major priorities. These signals should guide experiments, but every customer opportunity must be validated independently.

## Why these first

Customer support, back-office document processing, quoting, logistics exceptions, and commerce data quality have a strong combination of high repetition, verifiable output, recoverable errors, and identifiable budget owners. Public 2026 industry evidence also shows customer support and back-office automation among the most common B2B AI deployments, while data quality remains a major barrier.

## Pricing strategy

Start with a paid pilot rather than a long enterprise contract:

1. **Diagnostic / proof-of-value:** $0–$500 only when needed to remove sales friction.
2. **Paid pilot:** $500–$3,000 for 2–4 weeks, with one KPI and a defined workflow.
3. **Production:** $500–$5,000+/month depending on volume and integration complexity.
4. **Usage:** add per-ticket, per-document, per-shipment, or per-action billing when the unit of value is unambiguous.
5. **Enterprise:** implementation fee + annual/monthly contract after ROI is demonstrated.

Outcome-based pricing is particularly credible for support because the market already prices some AI agents per resolved conversation; hybrid subscription + usage is also established.

## First 3 experiments

### Experiment A — Support Resolution Engine
Build a provider-neutral mini app that accepts a ticket and returns:
- intent/category
- customer/order context from mock data
- policy-grounded answer
- confidence score
- human escalation decision
- draft response

**Success gate:** process 100 synthetic tickets and measure classification accuracy, safe-resolution rate, latency, and estimated cost per resolved ticket.

### Experiment B — Invoice/PO Exception Engine
Input invoice text + PO JSON. Extract fields, normalize supplier/amount/date, compare to PO, and produce `MATCH`, `REVIEW`, or `REJECT` with reasons.

**Success gate:** 100 synthetic documents; measure field accuracy, match accuracy, review rate, and estimated labor saved.

### Experiment C — RFQ-to-Quote Engine
Input a customer RFQ email/PDF text. Extract SKU/quantity/specification/deadline, identify missing information, and produce a structured quote draft for human approval.

**Success gate:** 50 synthetic RFQs; measure extraction accuracy, missing-field detection, quote preparation time, and error rate.

## Sales math

A simple pilot offer can be framed as:

`Monthly customer cost = volume × current manual cost/unit`

`Expected savings = avoidable manual cost + error/rework cost + protected revenue`

`Pilot price <= 20–30% of conservative first-year value` is a starting commercial heuristic, not a universal rule.

Example: 5,000 tickets/month × $4 avoidable handling cost = $20,000/month baseline. If a pilot safely resolves 30% without human handling, gross avoidable labor value is roughly $6,000/month before implementation/API costs. A $1,000–$2,000 pilot becomes economically testable.

## Important constraint

Do not claim customer savings before measuring the customer's baseline. Public AI ROI figures are heterogeneous and many are vendor-reported. The lab must measure each workflow using a baseline, controlled test set, API cost, latency, failure modes, and human-review rate.

# Support Resolution Resolver Contract

The resolver is the decision layer between Chatwoot and customer/order systems.

## Flow
Chatwoot event -> normalize -> classify -> retrieve approved context -> policy gate -> draft -> human review/auto-resolve candidate.

## Safety contract
- No order/customer context means no evidence-backed resolution.
- Risky intents (refund, payment, account access, cancellation, complaint) remain human-reviewed.
- Auto-resolution is opt-in per intent and requires an explicit confidence threshold.
- The resolver never invents order facts.
- The first commercial pilot should use `human_review` for every outbound action.
- A downstream adapter must deduplicate Chatwoot `eventId` before calling the resolver.

## Integration boundary
Implement `contextProvider({ticket, classification})` against the client's real order/CRM system. Implement `policyProvider(ticket)` against the client's written support policy. These providers are deliberately injected so EASY does not pretend a mock order database is production data.

## Current state
The resolver and tests are production-shaped decision logic, but **not a live customer integration**. Live pilot proof still requires a real Chatwoot instance, real order/customer source, written client policy, and human-approved outbound flow.
